title: From a 6'7" Bearskin Giant to a Gap-Toothed Prince: Inside the Pomp and Poignancy of Trooping the Colour
summary: Imagine standing on a balcony as 1,400 soldiers, 200 horses, and 400 musicians march below you, while jets scream overhead in perfect formation. That was the scene at Buckingham Palace on Saturday for Trooping the Colour, one of the year's most spectacular royal events. The ceremony marks the monarch's official birthday with a display of military precision and tradition. This year, the King and Queen Camilla were joined by the Prince and Princess of Wales and their children. Prince Louis, eight, has a history of stealing the show with his animated expressions, but this time he was on his best behavior, chatting with his parents as the Red Arrows flew past. The parade's name comes from "trooping" the "colour"—carrying a regiment's flag through the ranks. The Grenadier Guards had the honor this year. The King wore their uniform, still bearing the cypher of his mother, Queen Elizabeth II. Queen Camilla, as Colonel of the Grenadiers, wore a red uniform dress and a black beret with a white plume. Among the soldiers, Second Lieutenant Alec Goschen was hard to miss: at 6 feet 7 inches, he towered even more in his bearskin hat, reaching 8 feet 6 inches. But the celebration was shadowed by sadness. Lance Bombardier Ciara Sullivan was meant to ride in the parade, but she died after a fall from her horse during the Royal Windsor Horse Show in May. Her comrades have paid tribute to her in recent weeks. The King inspected the troops and received a 41-gun salute before leading the guards back to the palace. The day was a reminder of royal continuity—Charles standing with two future kings, William and George—and of the human cost behind the pageantry.
why_it_matters: This story shows how centuries‑old traditions still shape national identity today, and that even the most glamorous public ceremonies are built on personal sacrifice and real‑life loss—reminding us not to take the people behind the uniforms for granted.

background_read: Trooping the Colour has marked the British monarch's official birthday since 1748, when the parade was first held in its modern form.
The Grenadier Guards, one of the oldest regiments in the British Army (dating back to 1656), traditionally take turns with other foot‑guard regiments to troop their colour.

Buckingham Palace (the official London residence of the monarch) has been the backdrop for the ceremony since the reign of Queen Victoria, and the fly‑past by the Red Arrows—the Royal Air Force's aerobatic team—became a fixture in the 1960s.
Queen Elizabeth II, who died in 2022, attended the parade every year of her record 70‑year reign except 1955 (due to a rail strike) and 2020–21 (pandemic).
The late Lance Bombardier Ciara Sullivan was a member of the King's Troop Royal Horse Artillery, a unit that provides ceremonial gun salutes and escorts.

perspectives.description: The parade celebrates military skill, national unity, and the continuity of the monarchy. For many, it is a feel‑good event that brings people together and showcases British heritage. Supporters argue that such rituals strengthen a sense of community and history.

Critics point out that the ceremony costs millions of pounds at a time of economic hardship, and that it glorifies an unelected institution. Others feel the genuine grief of Ciara Sullivan's death was sadly overshadowed by the spectacle, exposing the monarchy's tendency to brush aside individual tragedy for image.

Historically, military pageantry has served to legitimize power—here, a new King under an old ceremony. The parade also highlights the tension between tradition and modernization in a constitutional monarchy where symbols carry real political weight, especially after the loss of Elizabeth II, a figure many felt was irreplaceable.

The presence of Prince George—a future king—raises questions about how the monarchy will adapt when Charles and William’s reigns are over. As the public's mood shifts, will spectacles like Trooping the Colour feel as relevant, or might they be scaled back in favor of a more modest, transparent royal family?
